newsitem.title: GERMANY: Italy aims to join EMU in 1999 - Ciampi in Spiegel.
newsitem.headline: Italy aims to join EMU in 1999 - Ciampi in Spiegel.

text.p: Italy is intent on joining the first wave of participants in European monetary union (EMU) in 1999, and is as committed as Germany to making the euro a stable currency, Finance Minister Carlo Ciampi said.

Asked by the weekly Der Spiegel whether Italy would be in EMU at the 1999 start, Ciampi said, "We are making every effort to reach the goal, not just because Italy was always deeply inspired by the spirit of Europe, and was one of the six founding members of the EU.
"We are also convinced that belonging to EMU will do good for our country as well as for Europe."

Ciampi indicated he would side with Germany rather than France in the debate over whether the euro should be primarily an instrument of stability, like the mark, or an instrument of trade competition against Asia and the U.S.

"We too place the highest value on stability. We need a strong, solid euro. With a weak euro we and other European countries would suffer the danger that capital flows would be diverted, bringing us higher interest rates. I do not believe one should use the currency as a weapon to promote exports."
Ciampi said critics of early Italian membership in EMU were wrong to think it would mean a weakening of the future single currency.

"This view perpetuates a false, outdated judgement. Looking at the entire postwar period, Italy was for a very long timne one of the most stable countries in Europe," he said. "In the 1950s and 1960s, inflation was very low despite a very rapid economic and social development."
After a period of instability starting in 1975 when wages were indexed to prices, Italy has now broken with the old thinking, he said. "We have accepted the culture of stability."
Inflation has been 2.5 percent since November, and Italy is making progress toward reaching the debt and deficit targets for participating in EMU.
"We have a high debt, but also plenty of private savings to finance it. That means no danger for other European countries. Our balance of payments is solid."
On the stability pact, designed to ensure that EMU participants maintain strict fiscal discipline after the start of EMU, Ciampi said he favoured sanctions, but opposed an automatic mechanism.
"The situation of a country, the deficits it can be forced to show, must be viewed in the light of political reason."

Asked what would be wrong with delaying EMU membership for a few years after the start, Ciampi said, "Italians believe in Europe even more fervently than the French or the Germans. That is why they are prepared to undertake every effort and sacrifice."

Public opinion in Italy is fully behind the goal of stability, he said. "I will admit, however, cutting the budget deficit by four percentage points next year will be a difficult hurdle, but it will be possible.
He said Italy would achieve this without creative accounting. "Italy has not engaged in windowdressing. Other members have," he said.
